t: Is Waiting An Effective Strategy When Students Talk During A Lesson nts-talk-during-a-lesson/
q: While it’s true that the strategy can help get wayward students back on track, it does little to ensure that it doesn’t happen again.
What may take just a few seconds of waiting in September takes nearly a minute in November. By January, it may not work at all.
The key is to pair the strategy with a clear and direct response.
John, Karla, Anthony, and Abigail, you each have a warning for breaking rule number two.
If, however, more than a few students are talking during your lesson, then it’s a sign that you’re either on the cusp of losing control of your class or you’re already there.
Because, either you weren't clear and detailed enough when you first taught and modeled how you want them to behave during lessons or you haven't been consistently holding them accountable.
More than a few, however, is on you, and a sign you must reteach and recommit.

t: How A Simple Preview Can Improve Behavior And Motivation or-and-motivation/
q: But in doing so, you pass up an opportunity to ensure that that next thing goes according to plan.
The way it works is that just before giving your signal to transition, you’re going to preview the next lesson or activity.
I’m going to be telling you an amazing story about a thirteen-year-old boy that you’re not going to believe.
Because when your students know what to expect, they’re able to relax, live in the moment, and focus on whatever you lay out before them.
And when you use the preview to sell what it is you have to teach them (#2), it can also be highly motivational.
When students don't know what to expect, on the other hand, when you dive straightaway into your lessons, they become antsy and excitable.
It comforts. It focuses. It builds anticipation. It opens the door to a class that is ready to learn.

t: How To Handle Students Who Question Your Methods -methods/
q: The questions may be different, but they’re all meant to challenge your methods.
Because if you become defensive, if you cross your arms and say “because I said so” or “because I’m the teacher,” you’ll put yourself at odds with your class.
Because, in this day and age, ‘my way or the highway’ doesn’t work. It merely seals your fate to a career of stress and battling with students.
By using the power of why , and appealing to the true reason behind your decisions, you can turn such questions around.
A great many students believe that teachers enjoy bossing them around—because that’s the conclusion they draw when you don’t provide the ‘why’ of what you do.
So when you get a question that is meant to challenge you or throw you off your game, seize it. Welcome it.
It’s an approach that sets you apart and demonstrates the purity of your motives. It causes your students to swim with the tide rather than against it.

t: Why Ambiguity Is The Enemy Of Effective Classroom Management assroom-management/
q: You’re going to remove all uncertainty over what does and doesn’t constitute breaking rules.
Enforcing consequences, then, becomes a well-choreographed dance, where both parties know their role, their steps, and their lines by heart.
Most teachers who struggle with classroom management, however, don’t go far enough. They don’t model enough.
But subtle doesn’t mean unclear. It doesn’t mean weak or wishy-washy. It doesn’t mean walking on eggshells or being inconsistent.
Your students must experience what it’s like to receive a consequence. They must know beyond a doubt what will happen—the precise script—every time they break a rule.
You don’t have to raise your voice. You don’t have to be aggressive or confrontational.
